title: Seeing Mingus in New York in 1973 and Willard's Mingus interviews
summary: At the 1973 Newport festival time she thought Mingus seemed distressed and unwell; Willard describes interviewing him in Los Angeles.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players

blocks.x: Newport.

The Newport Jazz Festival. And at that time Mayor Lindsay had a program on Sunday. It was a, you know, program with people from different walks of life, and by the festival starting at just about that time, well I think he had several folks there from the jazz festival. He interviewed them on his show. And Charlie Mingus was there and I think -- oh, I can't think of the other trumpet player's name right now, but another very fine trumpet player was on there, and several -- well, about four or five of the other musicians were there, guys that I knew them -- I remembered them by name, but I didn't know them as well as I knew Mingus, because I knew Mingus here. I met him on the coast. And at that time I sort of noticed a little something about Mingus that sort of bothered me. He seemed to not have been in command, you know, of himself. He seemed as though he was worried about something. He seemed a little distressed about something. I don't think he was well at that time. I think his passing recently, probably he was getting into this then, you know.
Yeah, it's very, very likely.

He was still performing, you know, and of course he was highly recognized, and -- but I have a feeling that he was never able to really do the things, or prove the things that he really had in mind proving, you know.
Uh-huh. Yeah. He was here in '73. He worked the new Shelley's Manhole.
Did he?
Yeah, he worked here for about 10 days, I think.
Uh-huh, in '73.
Uh-huh.
And then I remember we took him out to a radio station, out to KBCA, for an interview, and he -- Gerald Wilson interviewed him, and he would answer in like, 'Huh? Huh?'
Yes, this is what I'm saying, yes.

But when Gerald could manage to dig something out of him, or challenge him, he would speak up and say a few things, and it was obvious that he had a lot to say, but he just couldn't bring himself to say it. So we set up another interview, and we got Buddy Collette, Brit Woodman and I think Red Callender out there, to all reminisce about --
Different --
And then Mingus got excited and he talked.
Uh-huh.
But it took a lot of --
It took this to prompt him to do so.
Yeah.
I don't know what it was, as I say. It

could be that he had, you know, he wasn't well or something, at the time, because he would -- seemingly he was in a daze at times, and sitting, just sitting there, talking to Mayor Lindsay, who was a very controversial person, you know, and very intereted. He's really very interested in jazz, you know. And I thought it was wonderful for him to devote a part of that program to the festival, you know. He was still the Mayor of New York at that time.

But I really noticed it, I noticed then, because when I came back to the coast I was telling some of the musicians, some people here, that I had seen Charlie, you know, and he and I had talked a little bit, but he didn't have too much to say, you know. He just sort of looked like he was kind of out of it, you know. He might have been worried about his health then. It might have been the beginning, you know.
